radar.title: Accelerating high-throughput catalyst screening by direct generation of equilibrium adsorption structures
radar.summary: Abstract The adsorption energy serves as a crucial descriptor for the large-scale screening of catalysts. Nevertheless, the limited distribution of training data for the extensively utilised machine learning interatomic potential, predominantly sourced from near-equilibrium structures, results in unreliable adsorption structures and consequent adsorption energy predictions. In this context, we present DBCata, a deep generative model that integrates a periodic Brownian-bridge framework with an equivariant graph neural network to establish a low-dimensional transition manifold between unrelaxed and DFT-relaxed structures, without requiring explicit energy or force information. Upon training, DBCata effectively generates high-fidelity adsorption geometries, achieving an interatomic distance mean absolute error of 0.035 Å on the dataset from Catalysis-Hub, which is approximately 70% lower than that of the current state-of-the-art machine learning potential models. Moreover, the corresponding DFT accuracy can be improved within 0.1 eV in 94% of instances by identifying and refining anomalous predictions through a hybrid chemical-heuristic and self-supervised outlier detection approach. We demonstrate that DBCata enables accelerated high-throughput computational screening for alloy catalysts in the oxygen reduction reaction, highlighting the potential of DBCata as a powerful tool for catalyst design and optimisation.

Bayesian Distributionally Robust Variational Inequalities: Regularization and Quantification
radar.summary: We propose a Bayesian distributionally robust variational inequality (DRVI) framework that models the data-generating distribution through a finite-mixture family, which allows us to study the DRVI on a tractable finite-dimensional parametric ambiguity set. To address distributional uncertainty, we construct a data-driven ambiguity set with posterior coverage guarantees via Bayesian inference. We also employ a regularization approach to ensure numerical stability. We prove the existence of solutions to the Bayesian DRVI and the asymptotic convergence to a solution as sample size grows to infinity and the regularization parameter goes to zero. Moreover, we derive quantitative stability bounds and finite-sample guarantees under data scarcity and contamination. Numerical experiments on a distributionally robust multiportfolio Nash equilibrium problem validate our theoretical results and demonstrate the robustness and reliability of Bayesian DRVI solutions in practice. radar.title: Strong Nash equilibria of core-selecting double auctions
radar.summary: We study core-selecting auctions for double auctions that incorporate package bidding. Unlike in one-sided core-selecting auctions, the core may be empty in more general double auction settings, and truncation strategies need not be amongst a bidder’s best responses. Nevertheless, we establish the existence of a core-selecting auction in which every imputation in the core with respect to true preferences corresponds to a strong Nash equilibrium. Specifically, for any core imputation, there exists a profile of truncation strategies that constitutes a strong Nash equilibrium and induces precisely that imputation.

radar.title: Dual Active Learning for Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
radar.summary: Aligning large language models (LLMs) with human preferences is critical to recent advances in generative artificial intelligence. Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) is widely applied to achieve this objective. A key step in RLHF is to learn the reward function from human feedback. However, human feedback is costly and time-consuming, making it essential to collect high-quality conversation data for human teachers to label. Additionally, different human teachers have different levels of expertise. It is thus critical to query the most appropriate teacher for their opinions. In this paper, we use offline reinforcement learning (RL) to formulate the alignment problem. Motivated by the idea of $D$-optimal design, we first propose a dual active reward learning algorithm for the simultaneous selection of conversations and teachers. Next, we apply pessimistic RL to solve the alignment problem, based on the learned reward estimator. Theoretically, we show that the reward estimator obtained through our proposed adaptive selection strategy achieves minimal generalized variance asymptotically, and prove that the sub-optimality of our pessimistic policy scales as $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ with a given sample budget $T$. Through simulations and experiments on LLMs, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithm and its superiority over state-of-the-art.

radar.title: Statistical Efficiency of Distributional Temporal Difference Learning and Freedman’s Inequality in Hilbert Spaces
radar.summary: Distributional reinforcement learning (DRL) has achieved empirical success in various domains. One core task in DRL is distributional policy evaluation, which involves estimating the return distribution η π for a given policy π. Distributional temporal difference (TD) learning has been accordingly proposed, which extends the classic TD learning in RL. In this paper, we focus on the non-asymptotic statistical rates of distributional TD learning. To facilitate theoretical analysis, we propose non-parametric distributional TD learning (NTD). For a γ-discounted tabular Markov decision process, we show that for NTD with a fixed-distribution generative model (at time t ∈ ℕ, sample one state s t ~ μ with μ min := min s∈S μ(s) > 0 and observe a single transition from s t ), we need Õ(ε −2 μ min −1 (1−γ) −3 ) interactions with the environment to achieve an ε-optimal estimator with high probability when the estimation error is measured by the supremum 1-Wasserstein distance. This sample complexity bound is minimax optimal up to logarithmic factors. In addition, we revisit categorical distributional TD learning (CTD), showing that the same non-asymptotic convergence bounds hold for CTD. We also extend our analysis to the more general setting where the data-generating process is Markovian. In the Markovian setting, we propose variance-reduced variants of NTD and CTD and show that both can achieve a sample complexity bound matching the state-of-the-art statistical results for classic policy evaluation. We validate our theoretical results through numerical experiments on an inventory management problem, illustrating the practical utility of distributional policy evaluation in risk-sensitive decision-making. To achieve the sharp statistical rates, we establish a novel Freedman’s inequality in Hilbert spaces. This new Freedman’s inequality would be of independent interest for statistical analysis of various infinite-dimensional online learning problems.
radar.summary_short: Distributional reinforcement learning (DRL) has achieved empirical success in various domains. One core task in DRL is distributional policy evaluation, which involves estimating the return distribution η π for a given policy π.

a novel cooperative graphbased multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for intelligent channel selection in IEEE 802.11 networks.The framework combines cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning with graph neural networks (GNNs) to form a model that captures interference-aware interactions between access points (APs) for adaptive optimization in dynamic WLAN environments.The authors radar.title: The Virtual Biotech: A multi-agent AI framework for therapeutic discovery and development
radar.summary: Drug development requires evidence integration across biological scales and modalities, but relevant tools are fragmented. We introduce the Virtual Biotech, an organization of artificial intelligence (AI) agents modeled on a drug-development company, with agentic divisions spanning target discovery, safety assessment, modality selection, and clinical development. We demonstrate its utility at three drug-development decision points. First, more than 37,000 agents annotated outcomes from 55,984 trials and found that drugs targeting cell type–specific genes were 48% more likely to reach market with 32% fewer adverse events. Second, it integrated multimodal evidence to propose a therapeutic strategy in lung cancer. Third, it analyzed a terminated ulcerative colitis trial and inferred potential mechanisms of failure. These results demonstrate that human-guided multi-agent systems can conduct transparent, multiscale analyses to inform therapeutic-development decisions.

Non-equilibrium resonance scattering in intramolecular charge transport drives conformational changes
radar.summary: Abstract Intramolecular charge transport is conventionally described as proceeding along a static ground-state potential, with the carrier acting as a passive probe of a fixed electronic landscape. Here, using alkanethiolate-based molecular junctions, we show that the carrier itself can drive conformational reorganization once the applied bias brings backbone-delocalized molecular orbitals into the transmission window. Combined electrical and in situ structural measurements resolve a threshold-activated transition to a gauche-defect state coincident with the onset of orbital-mediated transport. We rationalize this coupling through a quantum resonance scattering framework in which accessible orbitals act as scattering potentials that transiently host the injected charge, depositing energy into nuclear motion with an efficiency set by molecule–electrode coupling and Franck–Condon overlap. The framework quantitatively reproduces the measured response and predicts the enhanced behavior of amide-containing junctions. Together, these results suggest that charge-transport–structure feedback can be understood in terms of microscopic parameters governing resonance-mediated energy transfer, and that these parameters may be tuned through chemical design.

radar.title: Financial Analysis and Auction-Based Congestion Management of Electrified Highways: A Case Study of Interstate 70 in the US
radar.summary: Abstract As the adoption of electric vehicles (EVs) accelerates, innovative charging solutions are needed to address range anxiety and infrastructure constraints. Dynamic wireless power transfer (DWPT) offers the potential to extend EV range while driving, enabling new forms of electrified roadways, but at substantial construction and operating costs. This study evaluates the financial viability of DWPT-enabled highways through a case study of a segment of Interstate 70 (I-70) in the US, with a focus on electric trucks. We propose a three-part fee structure consisting of a base fee for cost recovery, an energy fee for electricity consumption, and a congestion fee determined through a novel auction mechanism designed to regulate peak-hour access and improve social welfare. Extensive Monte Carlo simulations are conducted to account for uncertainty in cost and demand conditions. We further compare the total operating costs of conventional trucks and electric trucks using DWPT lanes across a wide range of scenarios. Results identify a traffic volume threshold on electrified lanes that governs economic viability. Below this threshold, electric trucks using DWPT roadways are more cost-effective in most scenarios, yielding mutual benefits for infrastructure developers and fleet operators. Above this threshold, the economic advantage diminishes rapidly with increasing congestion but can be mitigated through lower electricity prices or restrictions on non-EV traffic.

radar.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming traditional productivity and task management systems by enabling intelligent assistance for task planning, prioritization, scheduling, collaboration, and decision-making. This paper presents a survey of AI-driven personal and collaborative productivity systems, focusing on intelligent task management, scheduling, meeting management, large language models (LLMs), AI agents, multi-agent systems, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Existing research is reviewed and classified according to the AI techniques employed, application areas, system capabilities, and limitations. The survey examines how these technologies support individual productivity as well as collaborative workflows involving tasks, calendars, meetings, communication, and shared knowledge. A comparative analysis is presented to identify the strengths and limitations of existing approaches. The study further highlights key research gaps, including fragmented productivity tools, limited contextual awareness and personalization, challenges in autonomous task execution and multi-agent coordination, and concerns related to privacy, security, reliability, and human oversight. Finally, emerging trends and future research directions are discussed toward developing more integrated, adaptive, trustworthy, and context-aware AI-driven productivity systems. This survey provides a structured understanding of the current research landscape and identifies opportunities for advancing intelligent productivity and task management systems. Keywords— Artificial Intelligence, Productivity Management, Task Management, Intelligent Scheduling, Large Language Models, AI Agents, Multi-Agent Systems, Human-AI Collaboration, Retrieval-Augmented Generation.

radar.title: Prompt Injection and Jailbreak Attacks on LLM Applications: A Review of Attacks, Defenses and Risk-Adaptive Protection
radar.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are now embedded in chatbots, coding assistants, search tools and agents, and this has exposed a new class of security problems in which attackers use ordinary text to override a developer’s instructions or to push a model past its safety training. This paper reviews the literature on these problems, focusing on prompt injection and jailbreak attacks. It organises attacks into a taxonomy (direct and indirect injection, manual, optimisation-based, LLM-driven, obfuscated, multi-turn, multimodal and training-time attacks), organises defenses into eight layers from alignment-time training to system-level controls, and summarises the benchmarks and metrics used to compare them. It then examines a theme that is discussed less often than attack and defense strength, namely the cost of defending: most published defenses are applied uniformly to every request, while research on LLM routing and adaptive moderation shows that matching effort to difficulty can save cost. The paper discusses risk-proportional defense as a design direction, and closes with open problems, including adaptive attackers, evaluation validity, over-refusal, multi-model deployments and agents. The review draws on more than one hundred papers and resources published between 2020 and 2026.

radar.title: Operational Simulation and Performance Evaluation of Electricity Energy Markets Using WoLF-PHC Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
radar.summary: As the share of wind and photovoltaic generation in power systems increases, renewable generation and storage are increasingly participating in bidding in electricity markets. However, fluctuations in renewable output, uncertain market prices, and intertemporal coupling in storage operation complicate bidding and increase operating risks. This study develops an electricity energy market simulation framework covering medium- and long-term trading and spot-market trading. The Win or Learn Fast policy hill-climbing (WoLF-PHC) algorithm is used to model multi-agent bidding, accounting for contract settlement, deviation assessment, operating characteristics of conventional units, and constraints on the storage state of charge. Joint renewable-storage operation and independent participation are compared in terms of policy convergence, participant operating profit, consumer procurement cost, renewable utilization, and storage operation. The case study supports the effectiveness of the framework and shows that market participants can develop stable bidding policies. Compared with independent participation, joint operation coordinates energy internally between renewable plants and storage facilities, improving system operating performance while reducing consumer procurement costs and promoting renewable utilization.

radar.title: Robust Auction Design with Support Information
radar.summary: A seller wants to sell an item to n buyers. Buyer valuations are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) according to a distribution unknown to the seller; the seller only knows that the support is included in [a, b]. To be robust, the seller chooses a dominant strategy incentive compatible mechanism that optimizes the worst-case performance relative to the ideal expected revenue the seller could have collected with knowledge of buyers’ valuations. Our analysis unifies the regret and the ratio objectives. For these objectives, we derive an optimal mechanism and the corresponding performance in quasi-closed form, as a function of the support information [a, b] and the number of buyers n. Our analysis reveals three regimes of support information and a new class of robust mechanisms. (i) When a/b is below a threshold, the optimal mechanism is a second-price auction (SPA) with random reserve, a focal class in earlier literature. (ii) When a/b is above another threshold, SPAs are strictly suboptimal, and an optimal mechanism belongs to a class of mechanisms we introduce, which we call pooling auctions (POOL); whenever the highest value is above a threshold, the mechanism still allocates to the highest bidder, but otherwise the mechanism allocates to a uniformly random buyer, that is, pools low types. (iii) When a/b is between two thresholds, a randomization between SPA and POOL is optimal. We also characterize optimal mechanisms within nested central subclasses of mechanisms: standard mechanisms that only allocate to the highest bidder, SPA with random reserve, and SPA with no reserve. We show strict separations in terms of performance across classes, implying that deviating from standard mechanisms is necessary for robustness. Lastly, we show that the same results hold under other distribution classes that capture “positive dependence,” namely i.i.d., mixture of i.i.d., and exchangeable and affiliated distributions, as well as i.i.d. regular distributions. This paper was accepted by David Simchi-Levi, revenue management and market analytics. Supplemental Material: The online appendices are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.02703 .

radar.title: Market competition strategy optimization model based on the fusion of quantum game theory and multi-agent reinforcement learning
radar.summary: In this paper, a market competition strategy optimization model that combines quantum game theory and multi-agent reinforcement learning is proposed, and its effectiveness is evaluated through simulation experiments based on synthetic Cournot competition data. The model enables multidimensional exploration of the strategy space through a quantum superposition state and combines the cooperation-competition mechanism of multi-agent reinforcement learning to achieve rapid convergence to the Nash equilibrium in dynamic games. The simulation results show that the proposed fusion model significantly improves decision-making efficiency, requiring only 24 policy adjustments to converge compared to the 105 times required by traditional multi-agent reinforcement learning methods, while achieving an average market share of 31.4% and an average monthly profit of 7.3 Units, which verifies the expansion ability and robustness of the model in a complex simulated state space. This model provides theoretical support for the transformation of market competition strategy from single-product competition to a more integrated and adaptive competitive-strategy framework. The simulation results suggest that the proposed model can improve market share, profit performance, and strategy stability under synthetic market competition scenarios, providing theoretical and computational reference value for market strategy optimization.
radar.summary_short: In this paper, a market competition strategy optimization model that combines quantum game theory and multi-agent reinforcement learning is proposed, and its effectiveness is evaluated through simulation experiments based on synthetic Cournot competition data.

radar.summary: Efficient and adaptive routing remains a critical challenge in dynamic network environments due to changing traffic conditions, network congestion, and link failures. Traditional routing approaches, such as Dijkstra and OSPF, rely on static or semi-adaptive mechanisms, which limit their ability to respond to real-time network variations. To address these limitations, this paper proposes an Agentic Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (AMARL) framework for intelligent and decentralized routing. In the proposed model, each network node operates as an autonomous agent capable of observing local network conditions, communicating with neighboring agents, and making cooperative routing decisions. A multi-objective reward function is designed to jointly optimize delay, throughput, packet delivery ratio, and packet loss. The framework enables dynamic adaptation to network changes without requiring global recomputation. Extensive simulations are conducted under varying network sizes, traffic conditions, and link failure scenarios. The results demonstrate that the proposed AMARL model achieves significant performance improvements, including up to 45% higher throughput, 35% lower delay, and over 50% reduction in packet loss compared to traditional methods. Furthermore, the model maintains higher reliability under link failures and exhibits fast convergence with reduced energy consumption over training episodes. These findings indicate that the integration of agentic intelligence and multi-agent cooperation provides a scalable, adaptive, and efficient solution for next-generation network routing. The proposed framework is particularly suitable for dynamic and large-scale network environments where traditional routing methods fail to perform effectively.

radar.title: Reusability report: multi-sample omics network inference operates in distinct robustness regimes defined by prior knowledge and data availability
radar.summary: Abstract Knowledge-constrained network inference enables the reconstruction of regulatory programmes from high-dimensional biological data, yet the conditions under which shared and context-specific structures can be reliably identified remain poorly understood. Pablo Rodriguez-Mier et al. recently introduced CORNETO, a framework for multi-sample constrained inference. Here we reproduce, evaluate and extend CORNETO in terms of robustness, identifiability and bias–variance trade-offs. Using dynamic haematopoiesis and stable cortical datasets, we systematically assess four network reconstruction paradigms while preserving the original method-specific evaluation procedures and benchmark definitions. We show that multi-sample inference generally improves robustness and reproducibility, although gains in predictive performance depend on biological context and the completeness of the prior network. To enhance stability, we introduce bootstrap aggregation and selective re-expansion strategies that improve consensus robustness and recovery while preserving context-specific signals without modifying the underlying optimization scheme or sacrificing generality. Across datasets and methods, our results reveal distinct inference regimes governed by sample availability, prior knowledge and regularization. Together, these findings position network reconstruction as a regime-dependent learning problem and provide practical principles for robust multi-sample biological network inference.

radar.title: Cursed Equilibria and Knightian Uncertainty in a Trading Game
radar.summary: We introduce a novel equilibrium concept that incorporates Knightian uncertainty into the cursed equilibrium (Eyster and Rabin, 2005). This concept is then applied to a two-player game in which agents can engage in trade or refuse to do so. While the Bayesian Nash equilibrium predicts that trade never happens, players do trade in a cursed equilibrium. The inclusion of uncertainty enhances this effect for cursed and uncertainty averse players. This contrasts general findings that uncertainty reduces trade but is consistent with behavior that has been observed in experiments.

radar.title: The Data-Driven Censored Newsvendor Problem
radar.summary: We study a censored variant of the data-driven newsvendor problem, where the decision maker must select an ordering quantity that minimizes expected overage and underage costs based only on offline censored sales data rather than historical demand realizations. Our goal is to understand how the degree of historical demand censoring affects the performance of any learning algorithm for this problem. To isolate this impact, we adopt a distributionally robust optimization framework, evaluating policies according to their worst-case regret over an ambiguity set of distributions. This set is defined by the largest historical order quantity (the observable boundary of the data set), and contains all distributions matching the true demand distribution up to this boundary while allowing them to be arbitrary afterward. We demonstrate a spectrum of achievability under demand censoring by deriving a natural necessary and sufficient condition under which vanishing regret is an achievable goal. In regimes in which it is not, we exactly characterize the information loss due to censoring: an insurmountable lower bound on the performance of any policy, even when the decision maker has access to infinitely many demand samples. We then leverage these sharp characterizations to propose a natural robust algorithm that adapts to the historical level of demand censoring. We derive finite-sample guarantees for this algorithm across all possible censoring regimes and show its near-optimality with matching lower bounds (up to polylogarithmic factors). We moreover demonstrate its robust performance via extensive numerical experiments on both synthetic and real-world data sets. This paper was accepted by Wolfram Wiesemann, data science. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.09021 .

radar.title: Large Language Model-Enhanced Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Autonomous Enterprise Workflow Orchestration via Graph Semantic Routing
radar.summary: Automated orchestration of enterprise workflows is a core technical challenge in digital transformation, and predefined rule templates adapt poorly once business scenarios change frequently. This work proposes LeMARLA, a multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) architecture enhanced by a large language model (LLM). An LLM-driven decomposition module parses natural language business instructions into a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of subtasks and re-decomposes the affected subgraph whenever execution feedback reports a failure. A graph attention network-based semantic routing module computes task-employee matching on a heterogeneous graph of tasks, employees, and skills. A MARL module learns a global coordination policy under centralized training with decentralized execution, and the routing matching scores enter the policy logits as a differentiable semantic prior, so routing and policy are optimized along a single path rather than in sequence. In a log-replay evaluation parameterized by twelve months of real enterprise workflow records, LeMARLA reached a task completion rate of 91.7%, an end-to-end latency of 30.4 min, a load balance index of 0.71 per minute and a routing accuracy at rank three of 82.6%, outperforming all eight baselines with a Holm-corrected p value below 0.001 over ten independent runs and exceeding the logged historical assignment by 3.2 percentage points of completion rate and 26.2% of latency, with gains of 3.7 percentage points and 30.3% against the simulator replay of that same assignment. Ablations quantified the contribution of each module, decomposition quality was measured against an annotated reference set, and performance remained stable up to 2,000 employees.

radar.title: Cooling fast and slow: Characterizing the effects of vitrification in cryo-EM and the subsequent recovery of equilibrium populations
radar.venue_raw: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
radar.summary: Single-particle cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM), a powerful class of techniques in structural biology with the potential to resolve molecular ensembles, requires that samples be vitrified to protect them from the high vacuum of the electron microscope. However, the effects of vitrification on biomolecular ensembles are unknown. To study them, we carried out extensive molecular dynamics simulations (over 50 ms) of the Trp-cage miniprotein at equilibrium and undergoing rapid cooling. We simulated seven cooling rates spanning three orders of magnitude, with the slowest coolings matching experimental rates. By inspecting molecular mobility and density-temperature trajectories for water with and without protein, we found that water vitrification is unaltered by the protein. To track protein conformation changes, and to relate them to kinetics, we made a Markov State Model (MSM) of Trp-cage from 5.4 ms of equilibrium sampling at 277 K. We observed that MSM states with a characteristic time longer than the duration of the nonequilibrium cooling tend to be more robust to artifacts induced by such cooling. Critically, although we observe that some states vanish in the equilibrium ensemble at 230 K, none do in our nonequilibrium cooled ensembles. To account for these perturbations, we developed a thermodynamic inference framework for recovering equilibrium populations from vitrified ensembles. These results indicate that cryo-EM has the capacity to be an accurate technique for the study of biomolecular ensembles.

radar.title: Uniform Value and Decidability in Ergodic Blind Stochastic Games
radar.summary: We study a class of two-player zero-sum stochastic games known as blind stochastic games, where players neither observe the state nor receive any information about it during the game. A central concept for analyzing long-duration stochastic games is the uniform value. A game has a uniform value v if for every [Formula: see text], Player 1 (resp., Player 2) has a strategy such that, for all sufficiently large n, his average payoff over n stages is at least [Formula: see text] (resp., at most [Formula: see text]). Prior work has shown that the uniform value may not exist in general blind stochastic games. To address this, we introduce a subclass called ergodic blind stochastic games, defined by imposing an ergodicity condition on the state transitions. For this subclass, we prove the existence of the uniform value and provide an algorithm to approximate it, establishing the decidability of the approximation problem. Notably, this decidability result is novel even in the single-player setting of Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs). Furthermore, we show that no algorithm can compute the uniform value exactly, emphasizing the tightness of our result. Finally, we establish that the uniform value is independent of the initial belief. radar.title: Distributed Nash Equilibrium Solution for Asymmetric Multiagent Pursuit–Evasion Differential Games via Reinforcement Learning
radar.summary: This article addresses an asymmetric multiagent pursuit-evasion (MPE) differential gaming scenario, where pursuers, subject to the presence of external disturbances and unknown dynamics, aim to collaboratively intercept escaping evaders. The core technical challenge lies in designing a distributed optimal gaming protocol for such incomplete-information MPE games in an adversarial environment while guaranteeing the attainment of the Nash equilibrium. To address this problem, a model-based differential gaming framework is presented to eliminate the coupled terms in the associated Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs (HJI) equations and accordingly derive a distributed Nash equilibrium solution for multiagent systems (MASs). To dispense with prior knowledge of the pursuers' dynamics, a data-driven off-policy reinforcement learning (RL) algorithm is devised to learn the pursuers' optimal strategies online. Finally, simulation results are elaborated to validate the effectiveness of the proposed gaming strategy.

radar.title: Shill-proof rules in object allocation problems with money
radar.summary: We consider an object allocation problem with money. The seller owns multiple units of an object and is solely interested in her revenue. Each buyer can receive at most one unit of the object and has possibly non-quasi-linear preferences over pairs consisting of object consumption and a payment. We study the seller’s incentives to increase her revenue by introducing false-name buyers, a practice commonly referred to as shill bidding . An ( allocation ) rule is shill-proof if the seller can never increase her revenue by introducing false-name buyers. A rule is a price-based weak priority rule if there is a profile of posted prices such that buyers who are willing to receive a unit at their own prices are allocated units in descending order of their prices. We establish that a rule is revenue undominated among the class of rules satisfying shill-proofness, strategy-proofness , and individual rationality if and only if it is a price-based weak priority rule. This characterization provides a foundation for posted-price rules based on their robustness to shill bidding by the seller.

radar.title: Coordinated Offloading: Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for the Edge-Cloud Continuum
radar.summary: The increasing demand for intelligent, low-latency services in edge-cloud continuum systems poses new challenges for dynamic and efficient task offloading. We propose a Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) framework for distributed task offloading under partial observability, where each device offloads only a portion of its computation to a target edge server while executing the remaining portion locally (partial offloading). The problem is formulated as a Markov Decision Process (MDP), where each device independently learns an optimal policy under partially observable system states. To address the non-convexity, high-dimensional state space, and continuous action space, we develop a multi-agent Advantage-Weighted Actor-Critic (AWAC)-enhanced Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)-based computation offloading algorithm. The proposed method combines the stable policy updates of PPO with an advantage-weighting mechanism inspired by AWAC to emphasize higher-quality actions during training. To encourage cooperation without inter-device communication, a shared global reward aligned with system cost is employed. Extensive simulations demonstrate rapid convergence and significant improvement in overall system cost compared with baselines, e.g., Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) and Deep Q-Network (DQN).

radar.title: EduAgent-RL: A Human-Centered Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Framework for Personalized Learning, Adaptive Feedback, and Student Performance Prediction
radar.venue: International Journal of Computer Applications Technology and Research
radar.venue_raw: International Journal of Computer Applications Technology and Research
radar.summary: Personalization in digital learning is often handled through separate components: a knowledge-tracing model estimates what a student knows, a recommender selects learning content, and a conversational tutor provides feedback. These components are not always coordinated as part of a single instructional decision process. Recent reviews of agentic and multi-agent AI in education show rapid growth in this area, but also point to a lack of longitudinal studies and carefully evaluated real-world deployments [3, 12]. To address this gap, we propose EduAgent-RL, a six-agent framework comprising Student Profiling, Learning Analytics, Content Recommendation, Assessment, Feedback, and Teacher/Supervisor agents. The agents are coordinated through centralized-training, decentralized-execution multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), supported by a knowledge-tracing state encoder, retrieval-grounded feedback, and an explicit human-oversight veto. The framework is evaluated on two public benchmarks, OULAD [14] and EdNet [2], against random, collaborative-filtering, classical machine-learning, single-agent RL, and RAG-based LLM tutor baselines. In the pilot evaluation, EduAgent-RL reached an AUROC of 0.83 and NDCG@10 of 0.71 on OULAD, compared with 0.74 AUROC / 0.58 NDCG@10 for the single-agent RL baseline and 0.79 AUROC / 0.63 NDCG@10 for the RAG-based tutor. The ablation results also showed the largest drop in performance when the knowledge-tracing encoder was removed.

radar.title: dITP shifts the assembly equilibrium of Kongming to activate NAD+ hydrolysis
radar.summary: Abstract The Kongming (Kom) system, consisting of KomA, KomB, and KomC, protects bacteria from phage infection. KomA collaborates with a phage enzyme to generate deoxyinosine 5′-triphosphate (dITP), which activates the KomBC complex to hydrolyze NAD⁺ and trigger cell death. Recent studies propose that dITP activates KomBC through a simple conformational change. Our findings instead reveal a more dynamic mechanism. Without dITP, KomBC complexes exist in equilibrium between tightly packed oligomers and loosely packed filaments, both inactive. Tight packing accumulates unfavorable electrostatic interactions without positioning catalytic residues for NAD⁺ hydrolysis, whereas loose packing relieves these interactions but leaves catalytic residues misaligned. dITP binding at KomB stabilizes tightly packed KomC cores in the filament while aligning catalytic residues. Therefore, a small-molecule signal activates signaling by shifting the assembly equilibrium of higher-order protein complexes toward a catalytically competent state.

radar.title: TraceRouter++: Causal Semantic Routing Realignment via Optimal Transport
radar.venue_raw: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
radar.summary: Despite their remarkable capabilities, large foundation models (LFMs) remain susceptible to adversarial manipulation. Current safety intervention methods primarily rely on the locality hypothesis, rigidly suppressing isolated neurons or features. However, harmful semantics manifest as distributed, cross-layer circuits, rendering localized ablations both brittle against complex jailbreaks and detrimental to general utility. To bridge this gap, we propose TraceRouter++, a routing-level safety intervention framework that explicitly traces safety-relevant causal routing pathways activated under harmful inputs and realigns their unsafe activation states. Our framework operates in a Discover-Trace-Realign paradigm: it first pinpoints a sensitive onset layer via attention divergence and disentangles dense activations into interpretable routing features using sparse autoencoders (SAEs). Subsequently, it maps these features to downstream causal circuits via feature influence scores (FIS). Crucially, departing from rigid suppression paradigms, TraceRouter++ introduces a constrained optimal transport (OT)-based soft routing realignment. By formulating safety intervention as a tractable coordinate- wise marginal optimal transport approximation, our method redirects unsafe activation marginals toward safe-reference marginals within causally identified routing subspaces while preserving non-selected coordinates at the intervention point. This mechanism safely redirects malicious semantic flows while leaving orthogonal computational routes intact. Extensive experiments across representative large language models (LLMs), multimodal large language models (MLLMs), and diffusion models (DMs) show that TraceRouter++ outperforms evaluated baselines, improving adversarial robustness while maintaining a favorable safety-utility trade-off.

Recursive Adversarial Engine: A Stability-Oriented Architecture for Reliable Large Language Model Multi-Agent Systems
radar.venue: International Journal of Advanced AI Applications
radar.venue_raw: International Journal of Advanced AI Applications
radar.summary: Large language model (LLM) based multi-agent systems are rapidly migrating from laboratory prototypes to production deployments in finance, scientific research, industrial digital twins, and urban scheduling. As deployment scales, however, a family of systemic pathologies persists: decision oscillation driven by zero-sum agent interactions, cascade propagation of hallucinated content, long-horizon behavioral drift, value misalignment, and unresolved inter-agent conflict. Existing orchestration paradigms, which rely on instruction dispatch, greedy optimization, or static rules, address only shallow coordination and provide no principled mechanism for convergence. This paper proposes the Recursive Adversarial Engine (RAE), a runtime architecture for multi-agent systems organized around three propositions: bounded adversarial interaction supplies the error-detection signal, recursive correction supplies the error-elimination mechanism, and dynamic checks and balances supply the stability guarantee. We specify a four-layer reference architecture comprising adversarial verification, recursive correction, checks-and-balances scheduling, and steady-state output, and we characterize its convergence behavior through a Lyapunov-style stability argument. A qualitative comparison with self-play, multi-agent debate, alignment, and consensus frameworks delineates the paradigm difference. Engineering implications for high-stakes domains, long-horizon robustness, auditability, and middleware integration are analyzed, and open challenges are identified.

radar.title: Mobility, coupled constraints, and equilibrium selection in a three-tier health system with two strategic layers
radar.summary: We study strategic coordination in a decentralized public-service system in which an upper-tier authority sets policy benchmarks exogenously, intermediate authorities compete horizontally, and local providers adjust implementation in response to performance-based incentives. Since local providers’ feasible choices depend on regional policies, we formulate the simultaneous benchmark as a generalized Nash game. The paper’s main analytical contribution is a closed-form characterization of how coupled feasibility constraints, asymmetric piecewise-quadratic benchmark losses, and projected local responses jointly affect equilibrium existence and structure. We characterize the admissible equilibrium configurations of the simultaneous benchmark, including economically relevant boundary generalized Nash equilibria, and identify three stabilizing policy levers:better-calibrated alignment premia, softer historical baselines, and a recalibration of competitive pressures across jurisdictions. We complement the theoretical analysis with Monte Carlo evidence on the Price of Anarchy and the Price of Stability and compare the simultaneous benchmark with a sequential extension solved as a subgame perfect Nash equilibrium. The Italian National Health Service provides the institutional motivation for the analysis.

radar.title: Public Signals in Affine Network Congestion Games with Uncertain Free-Flow Times
radar.summary: Travel times in road networks are subject to stochastic uncertainty resulting from various parameters. A benevolent mobility service provider observing the actual travel times from data may use its informational advantage to steer the traffic equilibrium in a favorable direction through a processs known as signaling or Bayesian persuasion. Previous work has shown that the underlying signaling problem can be NP-hard to approximate better than [Formula: see text], even for static Wardrop flows with affine cost functions with stochastic offsets. In contrast, we show that in this case, the signaling problem is easy for many networks. First, we tightly characterize the class of single-commodity networks in which full information revelation is always an optimal signaling strategy. Second, we construct a reduction from optimal signaling to computing an optimal collection of active edges for the Wardrop equilibrium. For two states, this allows us to efficiently compute an optimal signaling scheme whenever the number of different active edge sets is bounded by a polynomial in the input size. Using a cell decomposition technique, we extend the approach to a polynomial-time algorithm for multicommodity parallel-edge networks provided that both the number of commodities and states are constant. radar.title: Strategic ignorance and information design
radar.summary: We study information design in strategic settings when agents can publicly refuse to view their private signals. Ignoring the constraints that agents must be willing to view their signals may lead to substantial divergence between the designer’s intent and actual outcomes, even in the case where the designer seeks to maximize the agents’ payoffs. We introduce the appropriate equilibrium concept — ignorance-permissive Bayes correlated equilibrium — and characterize implementable distributions over states and actions. The designer’s optimal response to strategic ignorance generates qualitative properties that standard information design cannot: the designer may provide redundant or even counterproductive information, asymmetric information structures may be strictly optimal in symmetric environments, providing information conditional on players’ viewing choices rather than all at once may hurt the designer, and communication between players may help her. Optimality sometimes requires that players ignore their signals with positive probability.

radar.venue_raw: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
radar.summary: 3D human motion-language alignment remains challenging due to the complex entanglement of spatiotemporal semantics. Previous methods typically rely on holistic alignment, which overlooks fine-grained structural primitives, i.e., body parts and sub-events, inevitably leading to imprecise correspondences and limited generalization. To address this, we propose MoLA, a unified motion-language pretraining framework that explicitly decomposes and aligns motion/language at chronological and structural levels. Leveraging large language models (LLMs) as prior knowledge experts, we reformulate the coupled textual descriptions into structured part- and event-level motion concepts, enabling precise supervision for fine-grained alignment. Based on this, we further develop novel chrono-structural alignment mechanisms to facilitate correspondence learning. At the spatial level, we introduce a part-mixture learning strategy that decouples body-part motions to facilitate part-decorrelated correspondence modeling. At the temporal level, we propose Gumbel-based adaptive consistency learning coupled with a chronological order objective to address this weakly supervised event alignment task. This enables the model to dynamically localize relevant motion clips and learn temporally coherent correspondences without requiring explicit boundary annotations. Furthermore, a directional consistency regularization is involved that models semantic relationships between global motions and their local patterns. Extensive experiments on motion-text retrieval, recognition, captioning, and generation demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods, verifying our motivation and effectiveness for unified motion pretraining.

radar.summary: Practice-oriented cybersecurity education often requires novice learners to build target web systems by hand before security analysis begins, imposing extraneous cognitive load. radar.title: Multiagent Assortment Optimization in Sequential Matching Markets
radar.summary: Motivated by the challenges faced by choice-based matching platforms, in this work, we study a generalization of the two-sided assortment optimization model. Specifically, this model consists of two sides (e.g., customers and suppliers) who have preferences over the opposite side in the form of discrete choice models. A matching is realized through a two-step process where the platform’s decision is to initially present to each agent on one side an assortment of users of the opposite side. The ultimate goal of the platform is to maximize the total expected revenue collected from the matching. Because of the computational complexity of this problem, we focus on the design of approximation algorithms with constant-factor guarantees for the constrained version of the problem under general choice preferences. First, to the best of our knowledge, we are the first to draw connections with the literature of submodular optimization and show that one-sided choice-oblivious approaches perform arbitrarily badly. Second, we show that, for the general setting, there exists a two-sided choice-aware randomized algorithm that achieves a [Formula: see text]-approximation factor, which is the best possible. Third, we design an algorithm that is asymptotically optimal when one side follows the well-known multinomial logit (MNL) choice model under the small probability regime. Fourth, we provide a simple and effective algorithm with a [Formula: see text]-approximation guarantee for the unconstrained setting, with both sides following MNL models. radar.title: Multi-AI agent framework reveals the “oxide gatekeeper” in aluminum nanoparticle oxidation
radar.venue_raw: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
radar.summary: Aluminum nanoparticles (ANPs) are among the most energy-dense solid fuels, yet the atomic mechanisms governing their transition from passivated particles to highly reactive states remain elusive. This stems from a fundamental computational bottleneck: Ab initio methods offer quantum-level fidelity but are restricted to small spatiotemporal scales (<500 atoms, picoseconds), while empirical force fields lack the reactive fidelity required for complex combustion environments. Here, we bridge this gap by employing a human-audited, multiagent framework to make the development and validation of a task-specific machine learning potential (MLP) more traceable and auditable. The workflow coordinates active learning, model evaluation, validation evidence, and human expert review, while leaving scientific interpretation and model-use decisions under researcher control. This collaborative cycle ensures quantum mechanical accuracy while exhibiting near-linear scalability. Strikingly, our simulations reveal a temperature-regulated dual-mode oxidation mechanism: At moderate temperatures, the oxide shell acts as a dynamic “gatekeeper,” regulating oxidation through a “breathing mode” of transient nanochannels; above a critical threshold, a “rupture mode” leads to shell failure and rapid combustion. Importantly, we resolve a decades-old controversy by demonstrating that aluminum cation outward diffusion, rather than oxygen transport, dominates mass transfer in studied regimes, with diffusion coefficients consistently exceeding those of oxygen by 2 to 3 orders of magnitude. These results provide an atomistic framework for interpreting ANP reactivity and illustrate how human-audited agentic workflows can make domain-specific reactive MLP development and deployment more reproducible.

radar.title: Optimal Power Scheduling on Cyber‐Physical Systems Subject to DoS Attacks: A Stackelberg Game Analysis
radar.summary: This article presents an optimal power scheduling strategy for cyber‐physical systems (CPS) vulnerable to denial‐of‐service (DoS) attacks. Departing from conventional Nash equilibrium approaches, we establish a Stackelberg game framework to model the strategic interactions between a multi‐type defender and a multi‐type attacker under information asymmetry, where both parties possess only probabilistic estimates of each other's total power resources. The work systematically develops optimal defense and attack strategies and proposes a Quantum‐behaved Particle Swarm Optimization (QPSO) algorithm to efficiently solve the resulting nonlinear, non‐convex optimization problem. To validate this method, we evaluated it in terms of rewards and convergence rates. Comprehensive simulation validates the effectiveness and superiority of the proposed approach.

radar.title: Personalized Privacy-Aware MARL Offloading in the Edge-Cloud Continuum
radar.summary: Task offloading in End-Edge-Cloud computing enables resource-constrained User Devices (UDs) to execute computation-intensive applications with reduced latency and energy consumption. However, existing task offloading schemes generally overlook the heterogeneous privacy requirements of users, leading to inefficient privacy-aware offloading decisions. In this paper, we propose a personalized privacy-aware task offloading framework, where the privacy requirement of each task is quantified through a User-Centric Privacy (UCP) model that considers task sensitivity, user privacy preferences, and task urgency. The task offloading problem is formulated as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) to jointly optimize the offloading ratio and the target computing server while minimizing the long-term system cost under latency, energy, and privacy constraints. To efficiently solve the resulting high-dimensional continuous optimization problem, we develop an Advantage-Weighted Actor-Critic (AWAC)-enhanced Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)-based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) algorithm under the Centralized Training and Decentralized Execution (CTDE) paradigm. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves lower average system cost, lower energy consumption, and higher task success rate than representative baselines under diverse privacy requirements.

Implementation via political parties
radar.summary: We address the implementation of public policies (alternatives) when the feasible set is unknown to the planner. The implementing agents are the political parties, who know the feasible set. They care about the implemented alternative, which reflects their ideology, and their share in parliament and office. They face a mechanism that, given the alternatives proposed by all parties, asks the voters to rank them and determines the chosen alternative and the shares in parliament and office. We identify conditions on parties’ preferences that guarantee the socially optimal policy is the outcome of the unique pure strategy Nash equilibrium of the electoral game played by the parties. The existence of the equilibrium does not require any assumptions about the parties’ ideology. To ensure uniqueness, shares must prevail over ideology: office or parliamentary shares in two-party systems, and strictly office shares in systems with more than two parties.

radar.title: Agentic workflows in large language models: a comprehensive review of architectures, planning strategies, and real-world applications
radar.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as agentic workflows: systems in which an LLM plans tasks, retains memory, uses external tools, and coordinates with other agents to complete multi-step objectives. Existing surveys typically evaluate these components in isolation or rely on flat, mutually exclusive categorizations that conflate coordination patterns with functional roles and tooling. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, this systematic review synthesizes 126 Scopus-indexed, peer-reviewed journal articles published between 2023 and June 2026, with screening conducted by a single reviewer. Because 122 of these articles appeared in 2025 and 2026, the corpus provides a timely, peer-evaluated evidence base for this rapidly accelerating field. Across seven research questions, we introduce a multi-layered taxonomy whose explicit novelty lies in strictly decoupling three primary coordination topologies (single-agent, collaborative multi-agent, and hierarchical supervisory) from orthogonal functional dimensions (role specialization), cross-cutting capability layers (tool augmentation and hybrid memory), and governance mechanisms (human-in-the-loop). Unlike prior rigid taxonomies that force systems into a single category, this structural separation systematically models modern hybrid implementations by combining distinct operational layers without artificial pigeonholing. Among the 57 empirical studies, collaborative multi-agent organization was the most frequently observed identifiable primary topology (27 studies, representing 47.4% of the empirical subset [ n = 27/57] and 21.4% of the total 126-study corpus). Across software engineering, healthcare, cybersecurity, and robotics, most reported implementations remain controlled research prototypes. Practical autonomy continues to be constrained by pipeline-level vulnerabilities: compounding error propagation, indirect prompt injection, memory poisoning, and the lack of standardized trajectory-level benchmarks. To advance agentic workflows toward dependable deployment, future research must prioritize standardized long-horizon evaluation, capability-based security architectures, and controlled self-evolution.

radar.venue_raw: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
radar.summary: While deep neural networks (DNNs) are being widely adopted, they are also increasingly exposed to model stealing risks, posing significant threats to intellectual property. Model fingerprinting, which utilizes intrinsic characteristics derived from the training process to authenticate models, has been proposed as a potential solution. An ideal fingerprint should satisfy robustness, uniqueness, and efficiency. However, existing methods often struggle to balance these three aspects simultaneously. To address this challenge, we propose TRUE, a twostage fingerprint generation and verification framework. In the fingerprint generation stage, we adopt adversarial examples as the fingerprint type and enhance their robustness through a minmax robust optimization strategy. In the fingerprint verification stage, we assign weights to the adversarial examples using a Boltzmann distribution to reflect their uniqueness, and further employ sampling based on these weights to reduce the number of queries and improve efficiency. Extensive experiments conducted on real-world datasets and across different model architectures demonstrate the superiority of the TRUE framework.

radar.summary: For multi-view data, structural heterogeneity across views is a common property, with cross-view sparsity variation serving as a typical manifestation. To first account for this sparsity-induced heterogeneity, we develop Adaptive View-specific Encoding, which incorporates the sparsity ratio of each view as prior knowledge for view-aware representation learning and constraint modulation. Based thereon, we further tackle the broader issue of view quality imbalance in multi-view fusion, where low-quality views introduce unreliable structural relations and view-specific constraints further amplify latent discrepancies. To this end, we propose a globallocal manifold-guided fusion mechanism named Early-to-late Manifold Consistency Calibration, which leverages the relatively stable global manifold preserved in early-fused encoded features to modulate robust late-stage fusion of adaptively encoded local features. Specifically, the early-stage global features serve as a structural anchor for assessing the manifold consistency of features of each adaptively encoded local view. The resulting consistency scores are then used to adaptively reweight late-stage global fusion, attenuating structurally unreliable views while reinforcing those aligned with the common manifold. In this manner, latent manifold consistency enables early fusion to calibrate late-stage fusion, thereby establishing a principled connection between adaptive view-specific encoding and cross-view distribution alignment. The full framework, named Manifold Consistency Guided Adaptive Sparse Autoencoder for Multiview Clustering (MASA), is validated on multiple datasets and demonstrates superior effectiveness and robustness across diverse experimental settings. On ALOI-100, MASA further enhances clustering stability, reducing the fluctuation standard deviation over the final rounds from 3.02% to 1.28%.

radar.title: A comprehensive survey of game theory models, applications, and future directions in cybersecurity
radar.summary: This survey provides a comprehensive examination of game-theoretic solutions for cybersecurity, charting the field’s evolution from foundational models to the emerging paradigm of autonomous strategic defense. We systematize the literature by classifying core game-theoretic frameworks, including Stackelberg, Bayesian, and cooperative games, and examine their application to critical security tasks. For each model–application pairing, we grade the supporting evidence as theoretical, simulation-based, benchmark-based, or operationally deployed, showing that most cyber-domain approaches have not yet been validated in operational deployments. A central contribution of this work is a critical analysis of the theory–practice feedback loop, illustrated through in-depth case studies of seminal deployed physical-security systems such as ARMOR, PROTECT, and TRUSTS, whose lessons we relate to cyber defense. These examples reveal how real-world implementation challenges, including adversary bounded rationality and environmental uncertainty, have exposed the limitations of classical models and catalyzed fundamental advancements in the field. Building on this analysis, we synthesize the convergence of game theory and artificial intelligence, providing a structured examination of three critical frontiers: the strategic arms race in adversarial machine learning, the design of incentive-compatible security for federated learning, and the development of adaptive defense agents via multi-agent reinforcement learning in modern cyber gyms. Finally, we analyze the strategic challenges of collaborative security through the lens of dynamic coalition formation models. By identifying key research gaps and charting a forward-looking agenda, this survey aims to equip researchers and practitioners with a nuanced understanding of how to architect the next generation of intelligent, adaptive, and strategically robust cybersecurity systems.

radar.title: Multi-Objective Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Urban Public Transport Fleets: A Systematic Review
radar.summary: Urban public transport fleets face challenges in balancing operational efficiency and passenger-related service quality. This systematic review, reported with reference to PRISMA 2020, synthesises 41 studies identified through five academic databases and search platforms between January 2018 and May 2026. The corpus encompasses direct public-transport applications, general Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) and Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning (MORL) research, and supporting literature from adjacent domains. The review examines MARL architectures, multi-objective reward formulations, coordination mechanisms, and operational outcomes while distinguishing application-specific findings from methodological insights. A conceptual Multi-Objective Partially Observable Stochastic Game (MO-POSG) formulation illustrates interactions between fleet-level objectives and passenger-related considerations. The synthesis discusses Centralised Training and Decentralised Execution (CTDE), value-based and policy-based learning, and scalarisation, constraint-based, and Pareto-based optimisation without assuming universal algorithmic superiority. Evidence from direct public-transport applications indicates potential benefits for coordinated vehicle control and service regularity, although reported passenger waiting-time, travel-time, and delay outcomes remain difficult to compare across studies. Offline MARL and conservative policy rectification are considered as potential approaches for limiting unsupported policy updates, without guaranteeing operational safety. Key deployment challenges include sensing uncertainty, adversarial vulnerabilities, and driver acceptance. Overall, the findings highlight limited application-specific validation and the need for transparent, comparable evaluation before broader real-world deployment.

radar.title: Q-Eval+: From Absolute to Relative Quality Evaluation for Text-to-Vision Content
radar.venue_raw: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
radar.summary: Text-to-vision (T2V) models are rapidly reshaping content creation, yet their outputs still require careful human screening before deployment in real applications. This creates an urgent need for evaluation tools that can 1) assign reliable absolute quality scores and 2) support fine-grained relative comparisons for model selection, reranking, and online A/B testing. Existing T2V benchmarks, however, are often limited by entangled definitions of visual quality and text-vision alignment, narrow coverage of images or videos, and the absence of systematically constructed pairwise and diagnostic annotations. Therefore, we present Q-Eval+, a large-scale dataset to jointly support absolute scoring and relative comparing for T2V content. Q-Eval+ consists of 220K image/video instances with 1.32M human annotations along two key dimensions: Q-Eval-Abs provides MOS-style labels for visual quality and alignment at both instance and model levels, while Q-Eval-Rel offers side-by-side preferences and choice-based VQA questions that reveal not only which instance is better, but also why. On top of Q-Eval+, we develop Q-Evaluator, a unified large multimodal model that bridges absolute and relative assessment through supervised fine-tuning with structured context prompts and a Vague-to-Specific alignment handling strategy. We further introduce symmetric and consistency accuracies to evaluate robustness under pairwise permutations. Extensive experiments show that Q-Evaluator achieves consistently strong correlations with human opinions and competitive comparative accuracy against existing open-source and proprietary LMM-based evaluators, providing a practical foundation for robust T2V quality control.

radar.title: Invariance, Stability, and Diversity: A Unified Framework for Multimodal Domain Generalization
radar.venue_raw: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
radar.summary: Multimodal Domain Generalization (MMDG) aims to learn models that generalize to unseen domains under unpredictable, modality-dependent distribution shifts. Despite recent progress, existing methods often rely on heuristic fusion strategies and lack a unified theoretical perspective, limiting their robustness under domain shifts. In this paper, we identify three fundamental challenges in MMDG: (I) insufficient cross-domain invariance across individual modalities and cross-modal interaction subspaces; (II) instability induced by asynchronous modality degradation, through which unreliable modalities impair joint representations; and (III) limited representation diversity, which exacerbates source-target support mismatch. To characterize these challenges, we derive a generalization error bound for a stability-weighted ensemble of modality-wise hypotheses, revealing three corresponding factors: Invariance (Source-Source Divergence), Stability (Stability-Weighted Error), and Diversity (Target-Convex Hull Divergence). Guided by this analysis, we develop a unified nonlinear fusion framework comprising Multi-Granularity Adversarial Alignment to promote invariance across modality-specific, interaction, and fusion spaces, Stability-Aware Adaptive Learning to prioritize reliable modalities during source training and mitigate asynchronous degradation, and Manifold Expansion to increase normalized source-feature dispersion as a source-side regularizer. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks show that our framework achieves the best overall average rank across 43 transfer tasks on seven datasets spanning four task families and eight diverse modalities.

radar.title: Mechanism Design for Contributor Governance in Crowdsourced News Platforms: Reputation, Role Promotion, and Phase-Transition Analysis
radar.summary: Crowdsourced news platforms rely on open contribution, so their content quality is vulnerable to malicious contributors—astroturfers (“water armies”), sockpuppets, and on–off sleeper accounts—that can poison content and manipulate the agenda at low cost. We formalize contributor governance as a mechanism-design problem that jointly combines a differentiated reputation-scoring model, a reputation-driven role-promotion hierarchy (editor, reviewer, aggregator, committee), and a reputation-weighted supermajority consensus rule. Using a discounted dynamic payoff model with an explicit multi-layer detection technology and evolutionary game theory, we prove that honest contribution is a Nash equilibrium under a penalty–quality–work ordering and a detection-dependent incentive-compatibility condition. Within a mean-field replicator model, we derive an explicit phase-transition threshold beyond which content quality collapses, with the tolerable fraction increasing in the penalty and the detection probability. We show that reputation filtering extends the one-third weighted-voting bound: when a fraction s of malicious accounts are sleepers and their selection-weighted average committee weight is κ times that of honest contributors, the expected-weight benchmark tolerates a total malicious fraction below 1/(1+2sκ) with a strict margin, which reduces to 1/(2s+1) when κ=1. We characterize the promotion threshold and the cold-start/Sybil trade-off. Numerical experiments comparing against no-governance, consensus-only, and EigenTrust-style reputation baselines confirm that the joint design combines weighted-voting safety with an extended tolerance.

radar.title: Preserved higher-order mentalising during strategic interactions after medial prefrontal cortex damage
radar.summary: Abstract Mentalising, the ability to infer the beliefs and intentions of others, is essential for successful social interaction. Previous studies have implicated the medial prefrontal cortex in mentalising, but whether this region is necessary for higher-order mentalising remains unclear. Here we show that people with focal damage to the medial prefrontal cortex retain the ability to engage in higher-order mentalising during a strategic social game. We compare their performance with patients with brain damage in other regions and lesion-free participants. Individuals with medial prefrontal cortex damage achieve similar rewards and use comparable mentalising strategies, but they are slower when making strategic decisions. Computational modelling indicates that this slowing reflects a greater tendency to require evidence before committing to a choice. Voxel-based lesion-symptom mapping identifies medial prefrontal regions linked to altered decision processes rather than mentalising. These findings suggest that the medial prefrontal cortex supports strategic decisions while higher-order mentalising remains intact.

Previous studies have implicated the medial prefrontal cortex in mentalising, but whether this region is necessary for higher-order mentalising remains unclear.

radar.title: Multitype Information Acquisition in a Strategic Trading Model
radar.summary: We analyze information acquisition in a strategic trading model with multidimensional uncertainties. Our main result is that the equilibrium can exhibit multiplicity because of the integer nature of the number of informed traders and the strategic interactions across different types of informed traders. We show that the number of equilibria can be arbitrarily large. Moreover, asymmetric equilibria can arise even in symmetric settings. As information costs rise, fewer traders acquire information, yet prices can become more informative. These results shed light on the instability of financial markets and yield testable empirical predictions. This paper was accepted by Lukas Schmid, finance. radar.title: Contest or Contract: Assessing the Effectiveness of Contests in Online Labor Markets
radar.summary: Online labor markets have become increasingly popular among companies seeking global access to workers. Some platforms have adopted a contest-based scheme, allowing employers to review multiple submissions before selecting the best one. This practice raises a crucial question: Given a predefined budget, should employers choose a contest or contract scheme for tasks? This study examines the comparative effectiveness of contests versus contracts in achieving better job outcomes, focusing on design tasks characterized by high uncertainty. Using a comprehensive data set from a leading online labor market, we employ multiple empirical strategies, combined with machine learning and text mining techniques, to examine the impact of compensation schemes on job quality. Our results suggest that contract-based jobs yield better performance than contests in the context of ideation tasks. Further analysis, such as examining image similarity among pairwise solutions within a task, identifies “copying” behaviors as a key mechanism undermining the effectiveness of contests. In the public setting of contests, workers can observe others’ submissions and revise their own, leading to imitation rather than innovation. As competition intensity increases, workers have weaker incentives to exert effort, reducing solution quality. Consequently, the negative incentive effects in contests outweigh both the potential positive incentive and parallel effects. Moreover, although information availability can enhance work quality, contests inherently offer limited informational advantages compared with contracts. Taken together, our findings suggest that contract-based schemes are more effective than contests for design tasks, offering important implications for both employers and platform designers in online labor markets. This paper was accepted by Karan Girotra, operations management. Funding: N. Zhang acknowledges the support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72302053]. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07082 .

radar.title: Nash Equilibrium-Driven Adaptive Behavior in Swarm Intelligence with Self-Organizing Maps
radar.summary: This paper proposes a swarm intelligence model that employs classical boid flocking dynamics combined with non-cooperative game-theoretic methods, specifically Nash Equilibrium, to simulate adaptive decision-making in multi-agent systems. The work leverages a payoff matrix based on fundamental flocking behaviors: cohesion, alignment, and separation, to enable each agent to dynamically optimize its own strategy based on local interactions within the group. The simulation introduces Self-Organizing Maps (SOMs) for clustering and behavior adaptation, providing a machine learning perspective on agent categorization and role differentiation. To simulate real-world unpredictability, stochastic noise is used to understand how varying noise levels influence collective alignment and coherence. The results demonstrate the impact of environmental factors on emergent swarm behavior and showcase the benefits of combining machine learning and game theory for adaptive control in distributed systems. This work provides valuable insights into the interplay between noise, decision-making, and flocking dynamics, with broader applications in robotics, swarm intelligence, and autonomous systems.
